transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I’m here because at school, when I see balloons—even just across the hallway—my chest tightens right away and I kind of freeze for a moment. It takes me a bit before I can think clearly about what I’m supposed to be doing.
Do you have this kind of reaction to things other than balloons?

No, not really other things. It’s mainly balloons. I know if there’s one in the classroom it’s probably just a decoration, but if it’s stretched tight or bobbing near the kids, I start thinking it could pop right in my face. It scares me more than it probably should.
How long have you been experiencing this reaction to balloons?
It’s been about seven months now. It started after a balloon burst really close to my face during a children’s art celebration.
Do you find yourself avoiding places or situations where you might see balloons?

Yes. Lately I’ve been trying to avoid them when I can. At school I’ll ask my aides to handle birthday circles if there are balloons, or I’ll move away from festival tables that have balloons nearby. If I really have to stay, I keep my distance and just try to get through it without looking at them.
Has your reaction to balloons been causing you significant distress or problems in your daily life or relationships?

Yes, it has. It’s starting to affect my work. I’ve had to hand off normal classroom celebrations to my aides when balloons are involved, and I missed helping with a festival art table I had planned because there were balloons nearby. My supervisor noticed, so… it’s becoming a problem.
Do you ever have memories or pictures in your mind of the balloon bursting that feel really vivid or disturbing?

I don’t think so. I mean, I remember that it happened, but I don’t usually get vivid pictures of it popping into my head or anything like that. It’s more that seeing balloons now makes me really tense.
Do you feel an overwhelming fear when you see a balloon, even if you know it's not going to pop?

Yes. Even when I know it’s probably just decoration and nothing is going to happen, if I see a balloon stretched tight or bobbing near the kids, I get scared. It feels like it could burst right in my face, and my fear feels bigger than it should be.
Do you ever feel like you're having a panic attack when you see a balloon?

It can feel close to that, yes. The second I spot balloons at school, even if they’re across the hallway, my chest tightens and I sort of freeze for a moment. It takes me a bit before I can think clearly about what I’m supposed to be doing.
Are there any other situations or objects, aside from balloons, that you avoid because they remind you of the balloon bursting incident?
Not really. I can’t think of any other objects or situations I avoid because of that. It’s mainly just balloons themselves.
Do you ever have flashbacks or feel like you're reliving the moment when the balloon burst near your face?
No, I don’t think so. I don’t really feel like I’m back in that moment. It’s more that seeing the balloon makes me tense and worried it might happen again.
Do you believe your fear of balloons is disproportionate to the actual danger they pose?

Yes, I do. I know logically a balloon in the classroom is probably just decoration, and it’s not that dangerous. But if it’s stretched tight or bobbing near the kids, I immediately think it could pop right in my face, and I get much more scared than the situation really calls for.
Has your fear of balloons affected your relationships with friends, family, or colleagues?

Yes, mostly at work. I’ve had to hand off normal classroom celebrations to the aides when balloons are involved, and I missed helping with a festival art table I had planned. My supervisor noticed, so it’s starting to affect things there.
Do you think your fear of balloons would improve if you were able to confront or be exposed to them in a safe and controlled environment?
I’m not really sure. I’d like to think that if it was really gradual and controlled, maybe it could help, but the idea of doing that still makes me nervous. I haven’t tried it in any formal way.
Do you think the balloon bursting incident was particularly traumatic for you?
Yes, I think it was. It’s really been going on since then—about seven months now—after a balloon burst close to my face during a children’s art celebration. That moment kind of stuck with me.
Do you avoid social gatherings because you're afraid of seeing balloons there?

Yes, if I think there might be balloons, I’ll try to avoid it or stay away from that area. Lately I’ve been asking my aides to handle birthday circles, and at festivals I’ll move away from tables if there are balloons nearby. If I absolutely have to stay, I keep my distance and just focus on getting through it without looking at them.
Do you often find yourself thinking about the balloon bursting incident when you don't want to?
I’m not sure I’d say often. It does come to mind sometimes, especially if something reminds me of it, but I don’t know that I’m thinking about it all the time when I don’t want to.
Do you often worry that something else bad or frightening might happen to you?
Not really in a general way. I mean, I worry about certain situations if they feel like they could startle me, but I don’t usually walk around thinking something bad is going to happen to me.
Do you ever have unwanted memories or images of the balloon bursting in your mind?
Sometimes, yes, if something reminds me of it. It’s not like it’s happening constantly, but I might get a quick picture in my head of it popping, and then I try to push it away.
Do you avoid thinking or talking about the balloon bursting incident?
I’m not really sure. I don’t usually bring it up on my own, but I wouldn’t say I’m actively avoiding talking about it all the time. If it comes up, I can answer, but I’d rather not dwell on it.
